config.title: Image Lazy Loading

intro.title: Image Lazy Loading
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a React component that efficiently loads images only when they are about to appear in the user's viewport, a technique known as lazy loading. You will learn the core concept of conditionally rendering content based on element visibility using the browser's Intersection Observer API. The main technologies involved are React functional components with TypeScript, the `useRef` and `useState` hooks for managing state and references, and the Intersection Observer for detecting visibility. By the end, you'll create a reusable `LazyImage` component that improves your app's performance by reducing initial page load time.
intro.usecase: Image lazy loading is essential for performance in content-heavy applications like e-commerce product galleries, social media feeds, and news/article websites. When users scroll through Instagram's infinite feed or browse Amazon's product listings, images load only as they enter the viewport, reducing initial page weight and improving load times. Developers implement this pattern in dashboards with data visualizations, portfolio sites with image grids, and any UI where numerous images could impact Core Web Vitals like Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define a structured type for image data with required properties
Implement React state hooks to manage the loading status of individual images
Use the Intersection Observer API to detect when images enter the viewport
Construct a custom hook to encapsulate lazy loading logic and make it reusable
Execute conditional rendering to display loading placeholders while images are not visible
Assign appropriate CSS classes to control the visibility and transitions of lazy-loaded images
Handle Intersection Observer callbacks to update component state when visibility changes
Utilize the useEffect hook to set up and clean up Intersection Observer instances
Control image loading behavior by conditionally applying the src attribute based on visibility
Define a reusable LazyImage component that accepts image data props and implements lazy loading
Invoke the custom lazy loading hook within components to enable lazy loading functionality
Modify image rendering to include fallback content or error handling for failed loads

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and useState into your component file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The import statement includes React
The import statement includes useState from 'react'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and state management capabilities.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package. Check your import syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the main LazyImage component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component called LazyImage that takes props with src and alt properties. The component should return an empty JSX element for now (like a div or fragment).
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named LazyImage that accepts props as an argument. Remember to specify the types for the props.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the LazyImage component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A LazyImage component is defined with typed props for src and alt, returning empty JSX.
successCriteria:
The code includes a LazyImage component (function or arrow function) that:
1. Accepts props with src (string) and alt (string) properties
2. Returns a JSX element (div, fragment, etc.)
3. Has proper TypeScript typing for the props
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the LazyImage component with typed props. This gives us the foundation to build our lazy loading functionality.
steps.feedbackPartial:
You're on the right track, but there might be something missing. Make sure:
- The component is named LazyImage
- It accepts props with both src and alt properties (both strings)
- It returns some JSX element
- The props have proper TypeScript types
steps.feedbackWrong:
The component isn't quite right yet. Remember to: 1. Create a function or arrow function called LazyImage 2. Define props with src: string and alt: string 3. Return a JSX element (even just a
) 4. Use TypeScript types for the props

steps.title: Define the component props interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'LazyImageProps' with two required string properties: 'src' and 'alt'.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and curly braces containing the property definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface that defines the shape of props your LazyImage component will accept.
successCriteria: The interface must be named 'LazyImageProps' and include both 'src' (string) and 'alt' (string) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the TypeScript interface for your component's props. This ensures type safety when using the LazyImage component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface includes both required properties with the correct types. Make sure you have 'src: string' and 'alt: string'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword, name it 'LazyImageProps', and include both 'src' and 'alt' as string properties.

steps.title: Initialize state for tracking image visibility
steps.instruction: Inside the LazyImage component, initialize a state variable called isVisible using useState, with an initial value of false. Make sure to use TypeScript generics to type it as boolean.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is: const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a state variable isVisible that tracks whether the image should be visible, initialized to false.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called inside the component
The state variable is named isVisible
The setter function is named setIsVisible
The initial value is false
TypeScript generics <boolean> are used
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isVisible state variable. This boolean will help us track when the image should become visible on the screen.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use useState<boolean>(false)? Did you name the variable isVisible and the setter setIsVisible?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to call useState<boolean>(false) inside the component and destructure it into [isVisible, setIsVisible].

steps.title: Create a ref for the image container
steps.instruction: Inside your LazyImage component, create a ref using the useRef hook to reference the image container element. The ref should be typed to hold an HTMLDivElement or null.
steps.hint: Import useRef from React, then declare a ref variable initialized with useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null).
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a ref that can be attached to the container div to track its visibility in the viewport.
successCriteria: Import useRef from 'react'
Declare a ref variable using useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a ref to reference the image container. This ref will be essential for detecting when the element enters the viewport.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported useRef from React and declared the ref with the correct type (HTMLDivElement or null).
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating a ref for the image container. You need to import useRef from React and declare a ref variable initialized with useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null).

steps.title: Define the intersection observer callback
steps.instruction: Inside your LazyImage component, define a function named handleIntersection that takes an array of IntersectionObserverEntry objects as a parameter and sets the isVisible state to true when the first entry's isIntersecting property is true.
steps.hint: Create a function that checks if the observed element is intersecting (visible in viewport) and updates the state accordingly.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleIntersection function that updates the isVisible state when the observed element becomes visible.
successCriteria: Function named handleIntersection is defined
Function accepts entries parameter typed as IntersectionObserverEntry[]
Function checks entry.isIntersecting property
Function calls setIsVisible(true) when intersecting
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the observer callback function that will trigger when your image container enters the viewport.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function properly checks the intersection entries and updates the state. Check that you're using the correct parameter type and calling setIsVisible when isIntersecting is true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleIntersection function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that takes IntersectionObserverEntry[] as a parameter and updates isVisible state when the element becomes visible.

steps.title: Set up the intersection observer effect
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook to your component that creates an IntersectionObserver to watch the containerRef element. The effect should call the observer callback when the element becomes visible and clean up the observer when the component unmounts.
steps.hint: Import useEffect from 'react', then use it inside your component. Create a new IntersectionObserver instance that calls your callback when the observed element intersects.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a useEffect hook that creates an IntersectionObserver to monitor when the container element enters the viewport.
successCriteria: Import useEffect from 'react'
Add a useEffect hook inside the component
Create an IntersectionObserver instance
Observe the containerRef.current element
Include a cleanup function that disconnects the observer
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up the IntersectionObserver effect. The observer will now monitor when your image container enters the viewport.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be something missing. Make sure you've imported useEffect, created the observer, observed the containerRef element, and included proper cleanup.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect for the IntersectionObserver isn't set up correctly. Review how to create an IntersectionObserver, observe an element, and clean up when the component unmounts.

steps.title: Return the basic container structure
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your LazyImage component, replace the existing div with a div that has the ref attribute set to containerRef.
steps.hint: Add the ref prop to the div element using ref={containerRef}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div element with the containerRef attached to it, which will be used to observe intersection.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div element
The div has a ref attribute
The ref attribute is set to containerRef
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully attached the containerRef to the div element. This will allow the IntersectionObserver to monitor when this container enters the viewport.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the ref is properly attached to the div element. Check that you're using ref={containerRef}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container structure isn't quite right. Remember to return a div element with the ref attribute set to containerRef.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering for the image
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, conditionally render an img element only when isVisible is true. Use the src and alt props for the image attributes.
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator or logical AND (&&) to conditionally render the image based on the isVisible state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component should only render the img element when isVisible is true, using the src and alt props passed to the component.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering based on isVisible state
img element with src and alt attributes
Uses props for src and alt values
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for the image. The image will only appear when the isVisible state becomes true.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're using the isVisible state for conditional rendering and that the img element uses the src and alt props correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't quite right. Make sure you're rendering the img element only when isVisible is true, and that you're using the src and alt props from the component parameters.

steps.title: Set image attributes from props
steps.instruction: In your existing conditional rendering, set the src and alt attributes of the img element using the src and alt props passed to your component.
steps.hint: Use the props directly in the img element: src={src} alt={alt}
steps.expectedOutcome: The img element will now correctly display the image source and alternative text from the component's props when isVisible is true.
successCriteria: The img element inside the conditional rendering should have both src={src} and alt={alt} attributes set using the component props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully passed the src and alt props to the img element attributes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're setting both the src and alt attributes using the component props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The img element needs to use the src and alt props passed to the component. Try adding src={src} and alt={alt} to the img element.

steps.title: Add styling for the placeholder
steps.instruction: Add a style prop to the container div to give it a background color and dimensions while the image loads.
steps.hint: Use the style attribute with an object containing CSS properties like backgroundColor, width, and height.
steps.expectedOutcome: The container div will have a light gray background and fixed dimensions, providing visual feedback while the image loads.
successCriteria: The container div has a style prop
The style prop contains at least backgroundColor, width, and height properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added placeholder styling to the container, giving users visual feedback while the image loads.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to include backgroundColor, width, and height properties in the style object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container div doesn't have the required styling. Add a style prop with backgroundColor, width, and height properties.

steps.title: Export the component
steps.instruction: Export the LazyImage component as the default export from this file.
steps.hint: Use the 'export default' syntax followed by the component name.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of default export for a component
export default MyComponent;
steps.expectedOutcome: The LazyImage component is now available for import in other files.
successCriteria: The component is exported using 'export default'
The export statement is placed after the component definition
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the LazyImage component as the default export. This makes it available for use in other files.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using 'export default' followed by the component name, and that the export statement is placed after the component definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't properly exported. Remember to use 'export default LazyImage;' after the component definition.
